newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Feb 20.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Feb 20.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- CLARKE HOPEFUL ON 2.5 PERCENT INFLATION GOAL

Figures from the Office for National Statistics have shown that retail sales in January rebounded by near record levels, increasing a seasonally-adjusted 0.6 percent from December. Compared to the same period last year, sales were up 4.6 percent, the highest increase since March 1989. Chancellor Kenneth Clarke welcomed the figures but insisted that he is still on track to meet the government's inflation target.
-- UK'S EMU ENTRY COULD BE DELAYED UNDER LABOUR

The shadow chancellor Gordon Brown has revealed a list of five 'British economic tests' that a Labour government would insist on implementing before taking Britain into European economic and monetary union (Emu). The announcement of the new set of hurdles means that sterling is likely to remain outside a single currency at the 1999 launch date regardless of which party wins the next general election. The Labour move followed comments on Wednesday from the foreign secretary, Malcolm Rifkind, that the government is 'hostile to a single currency'.
-- COPPER PRICES BOOSTED BY MARKET BATTLE

Copper prices have returned to levels comparable to those just before the Sumitomo scandal last June, when fears that the Japanese company might have had to dispose of huge stocks of copper sent prices tumbling by $1000 a tonne to $1,745. The price fall was triggered by the discovery of unauthorised trading by Sumitomo's chief copper trader, Yasuo Hamanaka, who is currently standing trial in Japan on fraud charges. A surge of buying on the London Metal Exchange on Wednesday saw the price of copper for delivery in three months - a benchmark price - jump by $74 to $2,360 a tonne.
-- STAFF REAP 57 MILLION STG PROFIT IN RAIL DEAL

The Labour party has seized on the sale of one of the recently-created rail rolling stock companies to again highlight the issue of 'fat cat' benefits to executives of privatised companies. In the deal, train leasing company Eversholt, one of three such companies sold by the government in January 1996 for a total of 1.8 billion stg, was taken over by leasing group Forward Trust for 788 million stg. Managers and employees at Eversholt netted a 57 million stg profit from the deal, prompting Labour to criticise the government for selling the companies too cheaply in the first place.
-- VIRGIN TO PUT 800 MILLION STERLING INTO WEST COAST LINE

Virgin Group has announced details of plans to invest 800 million stg on the west coast main line rail service which operates between London and Scotland. Virgin, which plans to increase ticket revenues fourfold on the line, is to invest 600 million stg in tilting trains to reduce journey times, and 200 million stg on improving stations and a telephone sales centre. After being awarded a 15-year franchise for the line, Virgin revealed plans to introduce seat-back video screens in new trains from 2002, and to provide airline-style services for passengers.
-- LONDON TUBE INVESTMENT OF 700 MILLION STG SHELVED

London Underground chiefs have told a Commons committee that the network has lost about 700 million stg in funds for core investment following a cut in government funding and cost overruns on the Jubilee Line extension. London Transport chairman Peter Ford warned the Commons transport committee that the cuts would affect virtually every line on the Tube network, with the threat of slower services and deteriorating trains, and would worsen an already serious maintainence backlog.
-- CLYDE FOUNDERS REGRET LOSS OF INDEPENDENCE

Several former directors in the UK oil company Clyde Petroleum, which on Wednesday lost its battle to resist a 494 million stg hostile takeover bid from Gulf Canada Resources, have confirmed that they sold their shares in the business, helping tip the balance in the Canadian's favour. Some of the former directors, including Clyde's founder Colin Phipps, expressed regret that the company had been taken over.
-- DAIMLER AGREES TO BUY FORD'S HEAVY TRUCK UNIT

Freightliner, the US truckmaking subsidiary of Germany's Daimler-Benz, has agreed to acquire Ford's US heavy truck business in a deal worth between $200 million (123.4 million stg) and $300 million (185.1 million stg). The deal, which represents a further rationalisation of the US heavy truck industry, will give Freightliner about 38 percent of the US market for Class 8 vehicles of more than 15 tonnes. The move, still subject to US anti-trust approval, will put pressure on rival truckmakers such as Navistar, Volvo and Mack to rationalise their operations.
-- US ARM POWERS ADVANCE AT MEDEVA

Pharmaceuticals company Medeva has reported a 31 percent increase in full-year pre-tax profits, to 103.5 million stg. The figures were boosted by strong sales growth from Medeva's Rochester subsidiary, which was bought last June for $370 million (228 million stg). A 65 million stg restructuring charge, announced at the time of the acquisition, hit Medeva's post-exceptional figure. Medeva's biggest-selling drug, methylphenidate, used to treat attention deficit disorder, saw sales rise 25 percent although the company warned of a sharp slowdown in growth of demand for the drug.
-- SB SET TO PAY $325 MILLION IN US SETTLEMENT

UK drugs giant SmithKline Beecham is reported to be about to settle a long-running legal dispute with the US government by paying $325 million (200 million stg) after being accused of falsely claiming payments from the US government's health service schemes Medicare and Medicaid. SmithKline said on Wednesday that it is not admitting fraud in the case, which centre's on the company's billing practices for the 100 million tests a year it performs in its clinical lab network.
